title: The influences of the transfer method and particle surface chemistry on the dispersion of nanoparticles in nanocomposites.
text_summary: 本研究通过原位聚合和表征，合成了由二氧化硅纳米颗粒（平均半径24.2±3.2 nm）在甲基丙烯酸甲酯（MMA）单体基质中制成的纳米复合材料（NCs）。首先，研究了两种转移方法（干燥和离心）以及不同的表面化学对球形二氧化硅纳米颗粒（NPs）在单体溶剂中的分散稳定性的影响。结果表明，干燥转移方法会导致NPs在MMA中形成大而多分散的聚集体，而离心转移方法则可制备出均匀的纳米复合材料，其中NPs以小而开放的聚集体形式均匀分布在整体NCs中。此外，通过在NPs表面接枝3-(三甲氧基硅基)丙基甲基丙烯酸酯（TPM）配体，可以进一步提高NPs的分散性，避免不可逆聚集，并增强NPs与聚合物基质的亲和力，从而确保NPs在聚合物基质中的均匀分散和分布。本研究结果为制备具有特定性能的纳米复合材料提供了重要的参考。

The inﬂuences of the transfer method and particle surface chemistry on the
dispersion of nanoparticles in nanocomposites†
Olivier Pravaz,a Beno^ıt Droz,b Peter Schurtenbergerc and Herve Dietsch‡*a
Received 13th July 2012, Accepted 11th September 2012
DOI: 10.1039/c2nr31846f
The synthesis via in situ polymerization and characterization of nanocomposites (NCs) made from
silica (SiO2) nanoparticles in a methyl methacrylate (MMA) monomer matrix is reported. We ﬁrst
investigate the transfer of well-deﬁned spherical silica nanoparticles (NPs) (average radius R ¼ 24.2 
3.2 nm) into the monomer solvent. We study the inﬂuence of two transfer methods and different surface
chemistries on the resulting colloidal stability. The ﬁrst transfer method consists of drying the silica
particles into powder before dispersing them via ultrasonication in the MMA matrix. The second is
based on repetitive centrifugations to exchange NPs from their synthetic milieu to pure MMA, avoiding
the dried powder state. These transfer methods are compared for two kinds of NP surface chemistry,
natural silanol (Si–OH) groups of the silica NPs and an additional silane coupling agent, namely
3-(trimethoxysilyl)propyl methacrylate (TPM), which mimics the monomeric group of the MMA
dispersing milieu. We then characterize the morphology of the resulting nanocomposites prepared
via in situ polymerization at a ﬁxed amount of dispersed NPs (2.2 wt%; 1 vol%) using a combination of
transmission electron microscopy (TEM) from ultramicrotomed nanocomposite ﬁlms,
thermogravimetry (TGA) and small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS).
Introduction
Nanocomposites are attractive materials that have increasingly
offered interest and possibilities for both fundamental research
and industrial applications.1,2 They consist of multiphase mate-
rials with at least one constituent phase having one dimension
smaller than 100 nm. Among the numerous possible combina-
tions of matter, inorganic/organic nanocomposites and more
speciﬁcally
polymer/silica
nanocomposites
are
the
most
frequently studied and reported in the literature.3,4 All facets of
synthesis, characterization of properties, and application of
polymer/silica nanocomposites have recently received increased
attention primarily because they ideally combine the best prop-
erties of both components. This allows for the preparation of
new materials with additional or enhanced features,1,3–6 such as
improved mechanical properties7–14 or a dynamic response to
external stimuli, namely electric or magnetic ﬁelds or tempera-
ture for example.2,15–17 Such materials have already been
employed in a variety of applications.3,4,15 It is common,
however, for thermodynamic and kinetic barriers to limit the
dispersal of inorganic nanoparticles, often hydrophilic in nature,
into organic polymeric matrices, often hydrophobic, leading to
NPs’ agglomeration.9 Thus, a major challenge remains in
reaching homogeneous and controlled dispersion and distribu-
tion of ﬁllers into the polymer matrix. Dispersion and distribu-
tion of integrated particles are often confused in the literature: a
good dispersion of nanoparticles is reached if there is no
agglomerate forms in the integrated matrix, whereas a good
distribution corresponds to an identical local concentration of
ﬁllers in all random volume taken from the overall material. For
some applications, the property enhancement of NCs relies on an
optimization of the ﬁller dispersion, such that the NPs–matrix
interfacial area is maximized. For others, one aims to produce
percolated networks or fractal aggregations of ﬁllers.18 In any
case, the resulting property improvements of nanocomposites are
partially or totally dependent on the ﬁller dispersion control and
quality into the matrix. The importance of the ﬁller’s dispersion
quality has mostly been demonstrated for the mechanical prop-
erties of ﬁlled elastomers or rubbers,11,13 but also of SiO2–
PMMA NCs.6 Thus, the effects of the compounding, the pro-
cessing conditions,7,9–11 and the surface chemistry12,18 have been
established as critical to the outcome of the NC’s properties. On
one hand, it has been shown that appropriate surface function-
alization may optimize homogenization of NPs into the polymer
matrix by increasing the mutual afﬁnities of the NPs and the
polymer to interact with each other.8 Usually, monomers or

polymers are grafted at surfaces offering steric repulsions
between ﬁllers and improving their afﬁnity with the matrix by
mimicking the polymer chemistry.19–22 On the other hand, even
when the dispersion is thermodynamically optimized by a ligand
addition on NPs’ surfaces, an appropriate processing strategy
should be employed.23 However, to the best of our knowledge,
only a few groups have reported on the effects of processing
conditions combined with the surface chemistry on the ﬁnal
dispersion, distribution of ﬁllers into the matrix, and/or the ﬁnal
properties of the nanocomposites.24
Here, we report a study on the inﬂuence of the method used to
transfer spherical model silica nanoparticles into a poly(methyl
methacrylate) (PMMA) matrix for two different surface chem-
istries of the nanoﬁllers. The concept of the study is schematically
presented in Fig. 1. For both types of surface chemistry, either
the ﬁllers are pre-dried or alternatively, their solvent is exchanged
by successive centrifugations before redispersion in the methyl
methacrylate (MMA) monomeric solution using ultra-sonica-
tion. After the transfer, a free radical polymerization is per-
formed. The effects of each transfer method are investigated
using both bare silica NPs with native silanol surface groups and
functionalized silica NPs with 3-(trimethoxysilyl)-propyl meth-
acrylate silane ligands on their surface.22 The two processing
conditions with two differently functionalized NPs thus lead to
the preparation of four new hybrid materials. The dispersion
quality of NPs into the matrix ultimately governs the ﬁnal
properties of the NCs and is a key property in the design of new
functional materials.5,14,25 We thus characterize the ﬁnal quality
of the NCs primarily in terms of distribution and dispersion of
ﬁllers into the medium through a combination of small angle
X-ray scattering and transmission electron microscopy.
Materials and methods
Materials
Tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS, 99.9%), absolute methanol
(99.8%), and ammonia (25%) are purchased from Merck. Azo-
bisisobutyronitrile (AIBN, 98%) and absolute ethanol (99.8%)
from Fluka; and 3-(trimethoxysilyl)-propyl-methacrylate (TPM,
98%) from ABCR. Ultra pure water (resistivity of 18.2 MU cm)
puriﬁed by a MilliQ system is used throughout the experiments.
All the preceding materials are used as received and without
further puriﬁcation. Methyl methacrylate (MMA, 99%) is
purchased from Aldrich and puriﬁed through a column ﬁlled
with aluminium oxide powder obtained from Merck.
Methods
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) is performed on a
Philips CM100-Biotwin microscope operated at 80 keV. Nano-
particles are visualized by concentrating the particle dispersions
using a lab centrifuge at 10 000 rpm, and drying a droplet of
particles disperse at about 1 vol% in ethanol onto a 300-mesh
carbon coated copper grid. The polymeric samples are ultra-
microtomed at room temperature using a Diatome diamond
knife on a Reichert-Jung UltraCut E Microtome to give 80 nm
thick sections. Sections are then transferred onto 600-mesh
copper grids for TEM imaging. Dynamic light scattering (DLS)
experiments are carried out with a 3D LS Spectrometer from LS
Instruments (Fribourg, Switzerland) equipped with a HeNe laser
operating at 633 nm. The DLS experiments are performed at
different scattering angles, q, ranging from 45 to 135 at a
temperature of 20 C. The mean hydrodynamic radius of the
polydisperse NPs is determined by the cumulant method.26,27
Small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) measurements are made at
the Swiss Light Source (Paul Scherrer Institute, Villingen, Swit-
zerland) and performed at the cSAXS beamline at 11.2 keV,
corresponding to a wavelength of l ¼ 0.111 nm, and with a
sample-detector distance of 8 m. The NPs dispersed in the
monomer are measured in 1.0 mm quartz cells and the fully
polymerized nanocomposites are cast in 1.0  0.1 mm thick ﬁlms.
Solvents and matrices are measured separately and subtracted
from the data. The two-dimensional SAXS patterns are radially
averaged and the resulting scattering curves are ﬁtted using the
software SASFIT.28 Elemental analyses of the NPs are realized
by the Zentralabteilung f€ur Chemische Analysen (ZCH) of the
Forschungszentrum J€ulich. For the quantitative measure of
carbon and hydrogen, 2 mg of dried non-grafted and grafted NPs
are burned in a CHNS analyzer (system LECO). The signals are
measured by IR-absorption of the ﬂux of CO2 and H2O gases.
The speciﬁc surface area (285.0 m2 g1), the mean pore diameter
(6 nm) and the total volume of pores (0.43 cm3 g1) of the NPs
are calculated following respectively the BET29 and the BJH
method.30 After 12 h of drying at 150 C in a Sample Degas
System (FlowPerp 060) from Micromeritics, the analyses of the
adsorption of nitrogen gas molecules at the NPs’ surface are
performed on a Surface Area and Pore Size Analyzer (Gemini V)
from Micromeritics. The ﬁller content of NCs is determined by
thermal gravimetric analysis (TGA) experiments performed
using a TGA/DSC1 SF110 STARe System apparatus from
Mettler Toledo equipped with a 70 mL aluminum oxide crucible.
Measurements are performed at a temperature rate of 10 C
min1 from 90 C up to 490 C with an air ﬂow of 300 mL min1.

In the crucible, the NC is heated until the mass remains constant,
only containing the ﬁllers as a residue. The ﬁnal mass divided by
the initial one yields the ﬁller content.
Spherical St€ober silica synthesis
Spherical St€ober-like silica particles are produced by the hydro-
lysis of TEOS in ethanol in the presence of water and ammonia.31
In a plastic bottle, water (2.4 mol L1), ethanol (13.9 mol L1)
and ammonia (0.5 mol L1) are mixed and the temperature is
raised up to 40 C under continuous stirring (650 rpm). When the
temperature is stable, TEOS (0.8 mol L1) is rapidly injected into
the mixture, and the reaction continues for 20 h at 40 C and
650 rpm. The particle size distribution is determined from a
statistical analysis of TEM images; approximately 1000 particles’
radii are measured and ﬁtted with a log-normal peak function.
TEM micrographs of the obtained NPs are available in the ESI
(Fig. S1†) and show spherical NPs with a mean radius of 24.2 
3.2 nm.
Nanoparticle surface modiﬁcation
The surface modiﬁcation is carried out directly in the St€ober
medium for 12 h under continuous mechanical stirring at
300 rpm. Short silane molecules of 3-(trimethoxysilyl)propyl
methacrylate (TPM) are grafted onto the silica particles surface.
As shown previously by 29Si NMR,20,32 grafted TPM is cova-
lently bonded to the NP surface due to the condensation of
ethoxy groups from the TPM agent with the silanol (Si–OH)
groups from the NP surface. Condensed TPM molecules then act
as steric stabilizers and improve the polymer–ﬁller afﬁnity by
mimicking the monomeric chemistry. The amount of TPM silane
agents is chosen to be in stoichiometry with the number of Si–
OH-groups present on the NPs surface (4 to 8 OH nm2 for
porous St€ober-silica surfaces33,34). Thus, 0.15 g of TPM silane
agents per gram of obtained silica NPs are introduced in the
St€ober medium. The resulting amount of grafted silane agents,
determined by elemental analysis, is found to be 3.2 nm2.
Transfer methods
In all experiments, a distinction between drying and centrifuging
transfer methods is made. The drying transfer method (D)
corresponds to the drying of nanoparticles in an oven at 100 C
for 12 hours, whilst centrifuging transfer (C) refers to the
exchange of solvent by means of successive centrifugation steps
(10 000 rpm, 10 min). After the synthesis of the nanoparticles, the
batch is divided in two parts. One is conserved as it is, and the
other is coated with the TPM-agent. Then, each batch is again
sub-divided into two parts in order to study the inﬂuence of the
transfer of nanoparticles into the monomeric bulk solution. The
ﬁrst sub-batch is dried in the oven followed by its dispersion into
the MMA by intensive sonication (2 hours at 45 kHz). The
second one is ﬁrst transferred to methanol and then into the
MMA by repeated centrifugation and sonication (30 min at
45 kHz) cycles. Centrifuged ﬁllers are thus never dried during
their overall transfer to MMA. For each solvent, the process is
repeated twice to ensure complete transfer.21,22 During the
transfer step, the content of silica nanoparticles is adjusted to the
desired volume fraction (4 ¼ 0.01), leading to ‘‘Hybrid
Monomers’’ (HM) of silica in MMA. The overall procedure is
depicted in Fig. 1.
In situ polymerization
A part of the hybrid monomer dispersions is then polymerized by
a free radical polymerization. Azobisisobutyronitrile (AIBN)
initiates to HM-dispersions at 0.1 wt% and is homogenized by
vortex (1 min at 1000 rpm). Under thermal conditions, AIBN
decomposition releases a molecule of nitrogen gas and forms two
2-cyanoprop-2-yl radicals used to initiate the free radical poly-
merization. The dispersions are then maintained at a constant
temperature of 55 C in an oven for 6 h, up to the complete
polymerization of the NCs or ‘‘Hybrid Polymers’’ (HP).
Results and discussion
Bare nanoparticles
To study the effects of the transfer method on the ﬁnal dispersion
quality, two systems are prepared and compared. Bare silica
NPs, naturally exhibiting silanol groups at their surfaces, are
transferred into the MMA bulk solution either after being dried
(D) or via successive centrifugations (C).
First, the stability of the obtained hybrid monomers (HMs) is
characterized by dynamic light scattering (DLS) measurements.
Mean hydrodynamic radii are found to be 70  6 nm and 76 
21 nm, respectively, for the systems transferred by centrifuga-
tions (CHM) and by drying (DHM). These values are roughly 2.5
times larger than the size of NPs in their synthetic milieu (30 
5 nm), revealing agglomeration of silica NPs in MMA. The mean
size for the DHM system is found to be slightly larger, and
indicates that DHM is more polydisperse than the CHM system.
The presence of a signiﬁcant aggregation is also supported by the
results from the SAXS experiments conducted with the two
samples (Fig. 2).
A portion of the HMs is then polymerized by a free radical
polymerization to create hybrid polymers (HPs). The dispersion
quality of the four obtained samples is characterized by small
angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) measurements. Three main
features are visible on the resulting scattering curves shown in
Fig. 2. First, for a given transfer method, one can see that the

data from the samples measured before (HMs) and after the
in situ polymerization (HPs) overlaps, suggesting that the in situ
polymerization step does not affect the dispersion and local
structure of the nanoparticles within the medium. Second, we
observe a clear deviation from the scattering pattern expected for
well dispersed individual NPs in particular at low values of q, i.e.
in the Guinier-region (q < 0.008 A1). Instead we ﬁnd a power
law behavior I(q) f qp that is typical for fractal aggregation.35
For fractals, p links the mass, M, and the characteristic object
size, R: M  Rp. Its value depends on the density of the NPs in
the aggregates or agglomerates.36 For each transfer method, a
speciﬁc exponent is found: p ¼ 1.85 for the centrifuged samples
and p ¼ 2.00 for the dried one. The drying transfer method
results in a steeper slope, i.e. larger value of p and thus a more
compact structure than the one obtained by the centrifuge
transfer method. The third feature concerns the structuring of
NPs in the medium. This is illustrated with the structure factors,
S(q), shown as an inset in Fig. 2 for the four samples. S(q) is
calculated through a division of the scattering intensity by the
form factor P(q) of the bare silica nanoparticles in ethanol.
Details on the determination of P(q) are given in the ESI.†
Brieﬂy, the experimentally obtained P(q) is well described by the
theoretical expression for homogeneous polydisperse spheres
with a mean radius R ¼ 24.5  3.2 nm and a log-normal distri-
bution. We do not observe a direct crossover from the fractal
behavior of the aggregates to the monomer form factor, but
instead observe a well pronounced correlation hole followed by a
weak peak at the typical nearest neighbor distance given
approximately by q* z 2p/2R. This pattern is again typical for
the scattering from aggregates and particle gels.37
Additionally, Fig. 3 shows TEM images taken with 80 nm-
thick ﬁlms that are microtomed from the HPs. These micro-
graphs show slices of ﬁlms cut from the upper and the lower parts
of the NCs. The slices from the upper part of the samples (Fig. 3a
and b) conﬁrm the aggregated behavior of the silica NPs in the
polymeric matrices. One can see aggregates consisting of about 2
to 15 NPs agglomerated in small and slightly opened structures
which are quite similar for both methods of transfer. Moreover,
differences in aggregates formed as a function of the transfer
method (mostly seen by scattering experiments) might lead to
sedimentation
in
some
of
the
samples.
Comparisons
of
microtomed-TEM images from the upper part (Fig. 3a and b)
and the lower part (Fig. 3c and d) of polymerized samples
highlight dramatic changes. Whereas the upper parts of samples
for DHPs and CHPs are quite comparable in terms of aggrega-
tion and quality of dispersion and distribution of ﬁllers in
PMMA, the lower parts of DHPs and CHPs are drastically
different. The micrographs taken from the bottoms of the
samples indicate that drying NPs leads to irreversible aggrega-
tion over the micrometer-range and subsequent sedimentation as
soon as the in situ polymerization starts. In contrast, the centri-
fugation transfer, which avoids any dried state, maintains a
rather
homogeneous
distribution
of
quite
monodispersed
aggregates throughout the whole sample. This is corroborated by
the photographs shown as insets in Fig. 3c and d which
demonstrate the higher opacity of the macroscopic DHP sample.
The large aggregates present in these samples are much larger
than the wavelength of visible light, resulting in a high degree of
scattering.
Finally, TGA analysis was used to quantify the mass fraction
differences in the upper part—where the SAXS curves are
measured—and in the lower part of the NCs. The CHP ﬁller
mass fraction is almost constant from the upper (2.2 wt%) and
the lower part (2.7 wt%). The mass fraction is only 20% higher in
NPs in the lower part, indication a quite low sedimentation
during the in situ polymerization. In contrast, the ﬁller mass
fraction in the DHP system is almost 4 times larger in the lower
part (5.8 wt%) than in the upper part (1.5 wt%) of the HP.
To summarize, the characterization of bare silica dispersed
either after drying or by exchanging the solvent into the mono/
polymeric matrix suggests that in situ polymerization does not
inﬂuence the dispersion state of NPs into MMA. Both transfer
methods lead to quite open agglomerates made of roughly 10
NPs. The drying transfer method is more inhomogeneous and
leads to slightly larger, denser and more compact structures in
the middle part of the sample and dense micron-sized aggregates
sedimented at the beginning of the polymerization in the lower
part of the sample. Moreover, the fact that the in situ polymer-
ization does not inﬂuence the ﬁnal dispersion and distribution of
the NPs in the PMMA matrix lets us to conclude that the largest
aggregates found in the DHP samples must have been formed
before the transfer into the monomer solvent (i.e. during the
drying of the NPs). Therefore we can exclude that depletion
interactions induced by the presence of the polymer could be at
their origin, contrary to what has been reported by Berriot et al.20
We believe that these aggregates are likely the result of irre-
versible aggregation caused by van der Waals (vdW) attractions
acting in the dried state. As a dry state can be avoided when
performing a transfer through centrifugation, we also expect that
irreversible aggregation due to vdW attractions can be mini-
mized. The small aggregates found in both CHP and DHP NCs
are however most likely the result of a lack of afﬁnity between the
hydrophilic character of silica surfaces and the hydrophobic one
of the MMA monomer.
These differences in the dispersion state of the resulting NCs
will most likely also inﬂuence their mechanical properties. In
2006, Oberdisse38 reported on a direct correlation between the
aggregation number and the mechanical reinforcement of bare
silica NPs in polymer matrices, at constant ﬁller volume fraction.
Thus, we also expect an improvement of the mechanical

Surface functionalized nanoparticles
To study the inﬂuence of the surface functionalization on the
ﬁnal dispersion and distribution of ﬁllers within a PMMA matrix
as a function of the transfer method, we have functionalized the
surface of silica NPs with a silane coupling agent, 3-(trimethoxy-
silyl)propyl methacrylate (TPM). The TPM ligand has the
double advantage of limiting irreversible NP–NP aggregation by
steric repulsion and considerably improving the NP–polymer
afﬁnity. The chemical behavior exhibited by the surfaces of NPs,
which consist of organic monomeric chains rather than silanol
groups, mimics the MMA monomer chemistry. As for the bare
silica NPs, the same transfer routes are applied to the TPM-
functionalized NPs, namely the drying and the solvent exchange
transfer. The volume fraction of NP ﬁllers in MMA/PMMA is
kept constant at 1 vol%. The grafting density of TPM is esti-
mated from elemental analysis to be 3.2 TPM molecules per nm2.
The stability and the mean size of the obtained HMs are
evaluated by DLS measurements. The mean hydrodynamic radii
are 36  7 nm and 37  9 nm for CHM–TPM and DHM–TPM
samples, respectively. These sizes show that the mean charac-
teristic size is independent of the transfer method, and quite close
to the value found for TPM–silica in ethanol (31  8 nm).
The HMs are subsequently polymerized in situ, in thin quartz
capillaries (1 mm thick), and their dispersion quality is then
characterized by SAXS. Fig. 4 shows the SAXS data obtained
when sampling in the upper part of HPs for both transfer
methods. On top of these curves, the form factor established for
the TPM-coated NPs in ethanol is also plotted (dashed line).
Details regarding the establishment of the form factor are dis-
cussed in the ESI.† For q > 0.004 A1, the experimental curves
perfectly overlap the form factor for porous NPs having a mean
radius of 25.0  3.2 nm. For q < 0.004 A1, small deviations from
P(q) are visible, highlighting minor but speciﬁc differences in the
dispersion of NPs, which depends on the method used to transfer
them into the matrix. The SAXS curve corresponding to the NPs
integrated
via
centrifugation
(CHP–TPM)
shows
a
slight
decrease of the forward scattering (I(q / 0)), indicating that the
NPs are homogeneously distributed in the matrix, resulting in
non-negligible positional correlations between the particles. In
fact, the best obtained ﬁt (full line) requires the contribution of a
hard sphere structure factor. This structure factor, S(q), obtained
by the division of the scattering intensity with the form factor, is
shown in the inset of Fig. 4. For q lower than 0.0035 A1, S(q)
slightly decreases below 1, which is characteristic for well
dispersed repulsive hard spheres at such an effective volume
fraction. The SAXS curve corresponding to the NPs transferred
by the drying method (DHP–TPM) shows an increase of the
scattering intensity at I(q / 0), which can be assigned to the
scattering contribution from larger objects or a result of attrac-
tive interactions. In fact, an additional contribution to the form
factor coming from larger homogeneous and dilute (S(q) ¼ 1)
spheres following a log-normal size distribution is sufﬁcient to ﬁt
the higher intensity at low-q. This second size is found to be quite
polydisperse, having a mean radius of 80  32 nm, and is
therefore attributed to small and dense aggregates. Nevertheless,
the number of these aggregates in the matrix is almost negligible
since they represent less than 0.025% by number of the total
scatterers. The plot of S(q) (Fig. 4 inset) shows a small increase
above 1 (q < 0.003 A1) with an apparent asymptotic value at q ¼
0 of S(q / 0) 2, suggesting aggregates consisting of only a few
monomers.
TEM images of the NCs are consistent with our interpretation
of the DLS and SAXS data. Fig. 5 shows microtomed-TEM
images for DHP–TPM and CHP–TPM from the upper and
lower parts of the samples (Fig. S3 in the ESI† shows additional
images at higher magniﬁcations). One can ﬁrst conclude that
excellent dispersion and distribution of the ﬁllers within the
matrix has been achieved independent of the transfer method
used for preparation. Furthermore, the picture for DHP–TPM
(Fig. 5a) shows the presence of some doublets well dispersed and
distributed in the matrix. Looking carefully at several micro-
tomed slices we see evidence for very few larger aggregates, as
shown in the inset of Fig. 5a. In Fig. 5c and d, TEM images are
shown for the lower parts of the HPs. The dispersion and

sample, indicating that almost no NPs are sedimented during the
polymerization step.
This result is conﬁrmed by TGA analysis, which reveals that
the ﬁller mass fraction is almost constant in the upper and lower
parts of the samples (2.2  0.2 wt%). It conﬁrms that surface-
functionalized NPs can be dispersed and distributed without
signiﬁcant aggregation and sedimentation, leading to homoge-
neously distributed NCs.
To resume, the good dispersion of the surface functionalized
NPs observed both with CH–TPM and DH–TPM samples is
most likely the result of two effects: ﬁrst, the steric repulsions
induced by the TPM–monomers covalently bound to the NP
surfaces reduces close contact between 2 NPs and thus helps to
avoid the formation of the largest aggregates due to vdW
attractions observed in the DHP NC. Second, the surface of the
TPM-coated NPs is no longer hydrophilic (like the bare silica
surface) but hydrophobic due to the methacrylate ending of the
TPM ligands grafted to the NP surface. In such conditions, the
afﬁnity for MMA monomers is considerably enhanced, thus
providing a good dispersion.
Independent of the method used to transfer the NPs in the
matrix, we expect the mechanical behaviour of these NCs to be
improved. The methacrylate part of the TPM agent (which is
covalently bonded to the silica surfaces)20,32 not only enhances
the compatibility with the MMA, but might be polymerized with
other MMA monomers. Therefore NPs act as cross-linker agents
for the PMMA matrix.
Moreover, as described by Singh et al.,39 well dispersed NPs in
PMMA are essential for high visible transparency material.40 The
transparency of such materials tremendously decreases when
aggregates with sizes larger than the wavelength of light are
present, since clusters of nanoparticles strongly scatter visible
light. We therefore expect that our ﬁndings are also highly rele-
vant for the preparation of nanocomposites used for optical
applications where high transparency is needed.
Conclusion
The study of the effect of the transfer method and the surface
functionalization of silica NPs on their quality of dispersion and
distribution within a PMMA matrix synthesized by in situ
polymerization has shown signiﬁcant differences. In situ poly-
merization is found to be an effective method to compound ﬁllers
into a polymeric matrix; moreover it allows the evaluation of the
NP structure in the monomer solvent as well as in the polymer
without modifying their initial dispersion and distribution. The
dispersion of dried bare silica NPs in MMA results in large and
polydisperse aggregates. The largest aggregates sediment at the
bottom of the sample, while the smallest ones remain suspended
in the matrix. Avoiding the dry state by exchanging the solvent of
the bare NPs via repetitive centrifugation leads to uniform
nanocomposites where NPs are aggregating in small open
structures that are homogeneously distributed in the overall
NCs. The ﬁnal dispersion of NPs is shown to be improved by
functionalizing their surfaces with a TPM ligand. This surface
modiﬁcation avoids irreversible aggregation by steric repulsion,
improves the NP–matrix afﬁnity by mimicking the organic
chemistry of the polymer, and, thus guarantees a homogeneous
dispersion and distribution of NP ﬁllers within the polymeric
matrices independent of the chosen transfer method. Therefore
the NCs described in this study may interest researchers who are
attempting to create model NCs in order to measure their
properties as a function of NC content and state.

image_summary: 这是一张示意图（流程图），图号为Figure 1，展示了二氧化硅（SiO₂）的功能化过程及基于该过程制备不同聚合物的流程。图中包含SiO₂的功能化（通过加入TPM实现），以及后续通过“转移”“干燥（MMA + 超声处理）”“离心（MMA + 超声处理）”“聚合（AIBN加热引发）”等步骤，分别制备出CHM、DHP - TPM和CHM - TPM等产物，各步骤以箭头和文字（如“polymerization”“transfer”“functionalization”）标注流程，直观呈现材料制备的工艺流程。

这是Figure 2，属于科学数据图，图表类型为散点图（主图）结合折线图（子图）。主图横坐标为q [Å⁻¹]，纵坐标为I(q) [a.u.]，展示CHM（方块）、DHM（圆圈）、CHP（三角）、DHP（倒三角）四种样本的散射强度I(q)随散射矢量q的变化，同时包含“fits form factor”（虚线）和“best fits”（实线）的拟合曲线；子图横坐标为q [Å⁻¹]，纵坐标为S(q)，展示结构因子S(q)随q的变化。主图中，不同样本的I(q)随q增大整体呈下降趋势，且不同样本的曲线存在差异，拟合曲线与散点数据匹配；子图中S(q)在q较小区域（约0 - 0.02 Å⁻¹）有波动，之后趋于平稳。

图3是科学图表中的显微图像，图号为Figure 3，图表类型为显微图像（包含透射电镜或类似显微成像）。图中包含a、b、c、d四个子图及中间的示意图：a、b、d子图展示分散的颗粒显微结构，c子图展示大量聚集的颗粒显微结构；中间示意图呈现一个装有蓝色液体和颗粒的试管，可能示意实验处理过程（如溶液中颗粒的状态或反应体系）。各子图下方均有1μm比例尺，左下角（c子图旁）和右下角（d子图旁）还配有圆形样品的实物照片，用于辅助展示样品外观。

Figure 4是一组显微图像（透射电镜图像），包含a、b、c、d四个子图及中间的示意图。a子图展示颗粒的显微形貌，带有500 nm和1 μm的标尺，左下角有局部放大图；b、c、d子图均带有1 μm的标尺，呈现不同条件下的颗粒分布形貌。中间的示意图为试管状结构，内部有蓝色和灰色元素，可能示意实验处理过程或样品制备步骤。各子图通过显微图像呈现不同状态下颗粒的形貌特征，标尺用于指示颗粒尺寸范围，整体展示不同实验条件或处理步骤下样品的显微结构变化。

图5是一张折线图，包含主图和内嵌子图。主图横轴为q [A⁻¹]，纵轴为I(q) [a.u.]，展示了CHP - TPM（绿色三角标记）、DHP - TPM（蓝色三角标记）的散射强度I(q)随q的变化，以及“fit form factor”（虚线）和“best fits”（实线）的拟合曲线；内嵌子图横轴为q [A⁻¹]，纵轴为S(q)，展示了结构因子S(q)随q的变化。主图中，I(q)随q增大整体呈下降趋势，不同样品的曲线存在差异，拟合曲线与数据点匹配；内嵌子图中，S(q)在q较小区域有波动，随后趋于平稳。
